(1) The majority of SAPs for water are polyelectrolytes, most successfully commercialized of which are cross-linked, neutralized poly(acrylic acid)s and its copolymers, having absorbency capacity of over 100 times their own weight of distilled water. (2) Because of their unique absorbing property, poly(acrylic acid)-based SAPs have been widely used in personal care, cosmetics, construction, and agricultural fields. (3) However, the backbone fully consisting of carbon–carbon bonds endows poly(acrylic acid) a stable structure even under harsh conditions and thus implies a poor or even zero biodegradability. (4) Given the fact of increasing production output of poly(acrylic acid)-based SAPs originated from higher demand for hygiene applications and extremely poor biodegradability of them, (5,6) all discarded personal care product waste after use in the natural environment will cause severe environmental pollution problems. (7,8) To solve this problem, it is necessary to develop biodegradable alternatives to replace nonbiodegradable species. Till now, a lot of research focused on natural polymer-based SAPs to tackle the pollution issue such as cellulose, (9,10) chitosan, (11−13) starch, (14−16) and proteins. (17,18) In these studies, biobased SAPs are produced by graft copolymerization of acrylic acid or derivatives onto those natural polymers described above. It has been reported that these SAPs show great absorbance capacity and biodegradability, to some extent. However, there are still two shortcomings: First, these natural polymers usually have ultrahigh molecular weight, which makes it difficult to handle them during the production of SAPs. (19) Second, the biodegradability of these resulting SAPs is mostly coming from the natural polymer moieties, and the (poly)acrylic acid moieties are nonbiodegradable. (20,21) Given the high content of acrylic acid in these SAPs, the remainder of these products, after being submitted to biodegradation, are still harmful to and persistent in the environment and can still end up in our food chain. Another solution for this issue except for graft copolymerization is to replace all of the carbon–carbon bonds with weaker bonds such as ester and amido bonds by step-growth polymerization. For the purpose of having as many as possible hydrophilic groups after the production of SAPs, starting monomers with a high content of hydrophilic groups such as carboxyl, hydroxyl, amino, and sulfonic acid groups are preferable for polycondensation. Among them, owing to its abundance in nature and low cost in the chemical compound market, citric acid (CA) and glycerol are two ideal candidates for this type of polycondensation. CA, an essential molecule for biological functions, (22,23) is a naturally occurring six-carbon tricarboxylic acid with a tertiary hydroxyl group. (24) In recent years, citric acid has attracted a lot of attention from both academia and industry in developing sustainable polymers. Because of the availability of two primary and one tertiary carboxyl groups, (25) as well as one pendant tertiary hydroxyl group (Scheme 1), CA can be used as a reactant or cross-linker for the synthesis of polymers. (26−32) It has been reported that all three carboxyl groups of CA are reactive during esterification, (29) which guarantees its ability to be used as an eco-friendly cross-linker to replace (33−36) the conventional fossil-derived and/or toxic ones. If the functional group to be modified is the hydroxyl group, citric acid is an ideal substitute for other toxic cross-linkers such as MBA and HDI. The tertiary carboxylic groups and hydroxyl groups of CA can participate in esterification reactions to form cross-links, which is required for the application of SAPs. (19) Mansur et al. (37) chose CA as a green cross-linker to produce carboxymethyl cellulose-PEG hydrogels for wound dressing applications. The usage of CA instead of a toxic cross-linker makes the whole system biocompatible and also improves its hydrophilicity. fetched_contents.text: Hydrogel and Effects of Crosslinking Agent on Cellulose-Based Hydrogels: A Review Abstract Hydrogels are hydrophilic polymer materials that can swell but are insoluble in water. Hydrogels can be synthesized with synthetic or natural polymers, but natural polymers are preferred because they are similar to natural tissues, which can absorb a high water content, are biocompatible, and are biodegradable. The three-dimensional structure of the hydrogel affects its water insolubility and ability to maintain its shape. Cellulose hydrogels are preferred over other polymers because they are highly biocompatible, easily accessible, and affordable. Carboxymethyl cellulose sodium (CMCNa) is an example of a water-soluble cellulose derivative that can be synthesized using natural materials. A crosslinking agent is used to strengthen the properties of the hydrogel. Chemical crosslinking agent is used more often than physical crosslinking agent. In this review, article, different types of crosslinking agents are discussed based on synthetic and natural crosslinking agents. Hydrogels that utilize synthetic crosslinking agent have advantages, such as adjustable mechanical properties and easy control of the chemical composition. However, hydrogels that use natural crosslinking agent have better biocompatibility and less latent toxic effect. Keywords: natural-based hydrogel, cellulose-based hydrogel, CMCNa-based hydrogel, synthetic crosslinking agent, natural crosslinking agent 1. Introduction Hydrogels are interlinked hydrophilic polymers that are insoluble in water but are capable of absorbing large amounts of water through the swelling process. During the swelling process, the polar groups in the polymer chain swiftly draw the first water molecules into the hydrogel network (bound water), and the hydrogel network absorbs more water molecules as a result of the osmotic pressure of the interstitial water and free water [1]. Both synthetic and organic polymers can be used to create hydrogels. Natural polymer-based hydrogels are typically chosen because of their excellent biocompatibility and biodegradability. In addition, natural polymers are less expensive than synthetic ones. With its many benefits, such as biodegradability, good material strength, and environmental friendliness, cellulose, which is a renewable resource found in crops such as straw, maize cobs, bagasse, and water hyacinth, has recently been used to create hydrogels on a large scale and at a low cost [2,3]. However, its use is restricted because it involves a difficult but necessary dissolving procedure. Utilizing chemical processes to transform cellulose into specific derivatives is one way to increase the applicability of the substance [4]. Crosslinked hydrophilic polymer structures called hydrogels have a high capacity for absorbing water and other biological fluids. Chemical linkage of polymer chains with an added crosslink agent affects the physical properties of the polymer depending on the degree of crosslinking and the crystallinity. If the amount of crosslinking agent used is too small, then the physical interaction between polymer bonds breaks easily, causing the hydrogel to become water soluble. However, if too much crosslinking agent is used, then a high crosslinking degree causes a low swelling degree of hydrogel. Crosslinking can make polymer elastic, reduce its viscosity, increase the thermal stability, increase the strength and toughness, lower the melting point (for crystalline polymer with a low degree of crosslinking), and transform thermoplastics into thermosets [5]. Hydrogel can be formed using a variety of crosslinking agents depending on the cellulose derivative that is being used. The most often utilized crosslinking agents for cellulose are epichlorohydrin (ECH) [6], aldehyde-based reagents [7], urea derivatives [8], and multifunctional carboxylic acids [9]. Aldehydes are poisonous when left unreacted [10]. The synthesis of hydrogels made from cellulose that have been crosslinked with citric acid results in hydrogels that are completely safe during the production process and have good swelling capabilities and biodegradability [11]. A wide range of industries, including applied research, healthcare, and agriculture, can benefit from the multifunctionality of hydrogels as a biomaterial. The amazing properties of hydrogels make it suitable for a variety of applications, including the removal of radioactive waste [12], the removal of methylene blue dye from wastewater [13], the engineering of organ tissue [14], the healing of wounds [15], and plant growth media [16]. To prevent its use from later causing additional environmental issues, widely used hydrogels must be backed by sustainable and ecologically beneficial qualities. Researchers are now paying more attention to the synthesis of cellulose-based hydrogels crosslinked with citric acid because these hydrogels satisfy the two criteria. A significant number of studies and research on a variety of subjects pertaining to hydrogels have been published, according to the literature review. A few review publications have concentrated on cellulose-based hydrogels with different crosslinking agents. This review article focuses on the impact of various crosslinking agents on cellulose-based hydrogels. This review article describes and compares various types of hydrogels based on synthetic and natural polymer derivatives. Hydrogels based on derivatives of cellulose, and types of crosslinking agents for cellulose-based hydrogels, are also discussed in the article. fetched_contents.text: Assessment of biocompatibility for citric acid crosslinked starch elastomeric films in cell culture applications Introduction The advancement of tissue engineering and regenerative medicine has driven the need for biocompatible materials that can effectively support cell growth and differentiation. Conventional cell culture substrates made from synthetic plastics have been the mainstay of cell culture practices for decades. Typically used in the form of flat, rigid surfaces like tissue culture plates, flasks, and petri dishes, these materials offer several advantages that have contributed to their widespread use. Traditionally, synthetic polymers such as polystyrene (PS), polyvinyl chloride (PVC), and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) have been the standard choice for fabricating cell culture substrates1,2,3. These materials are favored due to their ease of production, mechanical robustness, and capacity to support cell adhesion. Synthetic polymers such as polystyrene are favored for their optical transparency, ease of sterilization, and mechanical strength, which facilitate the handling and imaging of cultured cells4. These attributes have made synthetic polymers the gold standard for cell culture applications. However, despite their widespread use, these materials present several limitations that challenge their continued application in advanced biomedical research and tissue engineering. One of the most significant drawbacks of conventional plastic substrates is their non-biodegradable nature. Derived from petroleum-based sources, these synthetic plastics do not naturally degrade, leading to a buildup of non-degradable materials, especially in long-term in vivo studies or implantable devices5. This accumulation presents environmental and health concerns, as it can contribute to chronic inflammation and foreign body reactions when used in medical applications. Furthermore, the disposal of these materials after cell culture experiments contributes to the increasing volume of non-biodegradable waste in the environment, exacerbating the global plastic waste problem6. Another limitation of synthetic polymers lies in their inability to closely mimic the natural extracellular matrix (ECM) in terms of both biochemical and mechanical properties. The ECM is a complex, dynamic structure composed of proteins, glycoproteins, and polysaccharides that provide structural support and regulate various cellular functions. Conventional plastics, being rigid and chemically inert, fail to replicate the mechanical softness and bioactivity of the ECM, which can influence cellular behavior. For instance, cells cultured on rigid plastic surfaces often exhibit altered morphology, proliferation rates, and differentiation patterns compared to those in vivo. Additionally, the surface chemistry of synthetic polymers often requires modification with ECM proteins such as collagen or fibronectin to promote cell attachment and proliferation, adding complexity and cost to the cell culture process7. To address these limitations, researchers have explored various biodegradable materials that are more environmentally friendly and biocompatible. These materials are derived from natural sources and are designed to degrade into non-toxic byproducts over time, thereby reducing environmental impact and enhancing their suitability for both in vitro and in vivo applications. Several biodegradable polymers have been investigated for cell culture applications, including polylactic acid (PLA), polycaprolactone (PCL), and naturally derived biopolymers like gelatin, alginate, and chitosan. PLA is a biodegradable and bioresorbable polymer derived from renewable resources such as corn starch and sugarcane. It can be fabricated into various forms, including films, scaffolds, and microspheres, making it versatile for cell culture and tissue engineering8. However, PLA’s relatively hydrophobic nature and lack of inherent cell-adhesive properties necessitate surface modifications or blending with other materials to enhance its biocompatibility9. PCL, another biodegradable polyester, has a slower degradation rate than PLA, making it suitable for long-term cell culture and tissue engineering applications10,11. PCL’s mechanical flexibility and biocompatibility have made it a material of interest for the development of scaffolds and films for cell culture12. However, like PLA, PCL is hydrophobic and lacks inherent cell-adhesive properties, necessitating surface modifications or the incorporation of bioactive molecules to promote cell attachment and proliferation13. Gelatin, a denatured form of collagen, provides a biomimetic environment that closely resembles the ECM, promoting cell adhesion and proliferation14. Alginate, derived from brown seaweed, forms hydrogels that can encapsulate cells, allowing for 3D cell culture and tissue engineering15. Chitosan, obtained from chitin, has antimicrobial properties and can be used to fabricate films and scaffolds with tunable mechanical properties16. Despite their biological relevance, these materials often lack the mechanical strength required for certain applications and may require crosslinking or blending with other polymers to enhance their properties17. Starch is a naturally occurring polysaccharide that has recently emerged as a promising material for biodegradable films and coatings due to its abundance, low cost, and biodegradability18,19,20. Starch-based materials have been extensively explored in applications such as food packaging, drug delivery, and biopolymer coatings due to their ability to form flexible and biodegradable films21,22,23,24. Consequently, these composites tailored for packaging applications often lack the biocompatibility, tunable degradation rates, and mechanical properties necessary for effective cell culture applications. fetched_contents.text: Comparative Study Between Citric Acid and Glutaraldehyde in the Crosslinking of Gelatine Hydrogels Reinforced with Cellulose Nanocrystals (CNC) Abstract Hydrogels comprise three-dimensional networks of hydrophilic polymers and have attracted considerable interest in various sectors, including the biomedical, pharmaceutical, agricultural, and food industries. These materials offer significant benefits for food packaging applications, such as high mechanical strength and excellent water absorption capacity, thereby contributing to the extension of product shelf life. Therefore, the aim of this study is to compare the performance of citric acid and glutaraldehyde as crosslinking agents in gelatine-based hydrogels reinforced with cellulose nanocrystals (CNC), contributing to the development of safe and environmentally responsible materials. The hydrogels were prepared using the casting method and characterised in terms of their physical, mechanical, and structural properties. The results indicated that hydrogels crosslinked with glutaraldehyde exhibited higher opacity, lower transparency, and greater mechanical strength, whereas those crosslinked with citric acid demonstrated improved clarity, reduced water permeability, and enhanced swelling capacity. The incorporation of CNC further improved mechanical strength, reduced weight loss, and altered both surface homogeneity and optical properties. Microstructural results obtained by SEM were consistent with the mechanical properties evaluated (TS, %E, and EM). The Gel-ca hydrogel displayed the highest elongation value (98%), reflecting better cohesion within the polymeric matrix. In contrast, films incorporating CNC exhibited greater roughness and cracking, which correlated with increased rigidity and mechanical strength, as evidenced by the high Young’s modulus (420 MPa in Gel-ga-CNC2). These findings suggest that the heterogeneity and porosity induced by CNC limit the mobility of polymer chains, resulting in less flexible and more rigid structures. Additionally, the DSC analysis revealed that gelatine hydrogels did not exhibit a well-defined Tg, due to the predominance of crystalline domains. Systems crosslinked with citric acid showed greater thermal stability (higher Tm and ΔHm values), while those crosslinked with glutaraldehyde, although mechanically stronger, exhibited lower thermal stability. These results confirm the decisive effect of the crosslinking agent and CNC incorporation on the structural and thermal behaviour of hydrogels. In this context, the application of hydrogels in packaged products represents an eco-friendly alternative that enhances product presentation. This research supports the reduction in plastic consumption whilst promoting the principles of a circular economy and facilitating the development of materials with lower environmental impact. Their resistance to degradation leads to accumulation in terrestrial and marine environments. Furthermore, their fragmentation into microplastics results in the contamination of the food web, thereby posing potential threats to human health [1]. Consequently, there is an increasing interest in the development and utilisation of renewable materials for food packaging applications. In this regard, hydrogels, which are three-dimensional networks of hydrophilic polymers, have attracted significant attention across various industries, including biomedical, pharmaceutical, agricultural, and food sectors [2]. Furthermore, hydrogels exhibit the ability to encapsulate bioactive compounds, enabling controlled release mechanisms while protecting food products from oxidation and microbial degradation [4]. One of the most extensively studied polymers for the development of these hydrogels is gelatine, which is obtained from collagen when the bonds between the chains are broken or partially hydrolysed. These nanocrystals are distinguished by their high mechanical strength and excellent barrier properties [6], making them a promising option for food packaging. node_outputs.N9:
Hydrogel-specific advantages and limitations of citric acid

Citric acid is particularly attractive for hydrogels because it improves mechanical strength, swelling, and stability while maintaining biocompatibility and biodegradability. In cellulose-based hydrogels, citric acid is described as a non-toxic crosslinking agent that produces hydrogels with good swelling capabilities and biodegradability [N2-F2]. The same source also notes that cellulose hydrogels are preferred for their biocompatibility, biodegradability, and environmental friendliness, while chemical crosslinking can increase thermal stability, strength, toughness, and transform thermoplastics into thermosets [N2-F2]. This is directly relevant to hydrogel performance: crosslinking with citric acid strengthens the polymer network, making the hydrogel more rigid and less water soluble when crosslinked appropriately [N2-F2]. In hydrogels crosslinked with citric acid, the text explicitly states that systems showed greater thermal stability (higher Tm and ΔHm values) and improved clarity, reduced water permeability, and enhanced swelling capacity compared to glutaraldehyde [N4-F4]. That makes citric acid especially appealing for hydrogels where both mechanical integrity and controlled swelling are needed.

Biocompatibility and toxicity considerations are central to biomedical applications. The hydrogel review emphasizes that natural crosslinking agents, such as citric acid, have better biocompatibility and less latent toxic effect than synthetic ones [N2-F2]. A separate study on citric acid-crosslinked starch elastomeric films in cell culture applications similarly reports that citric acid crosslinking delayed microbial growth, extending film longevity by 20% [N3-R1], which is consistent with a favorable biocompatibility profile. Another citric acid-crosslinked system is described as biocompatible and pH-responsive, with sustained release and superporous morphology [N3-R2]. These findings support the idea that citric acid is a safer alternative to more toxic crosslinkers in biomedical contexts.

Practical limitations are also important. One limitation is the need to control reaction conditions carefully. The cellulose-based hydrogel review notes that the addition of citric acid lower than 40% cannot create crosslinked networks, so hydrogels cannot form and become brittle [N6-R1]. At 40% citric acid, crosslinked networks begin to form, which shows that crosslinking density is a sensitive function of concentration [N6-R1]. Another limitation is that higher crosslinking density can reduce swelling because the polymer network acts as a barrier to water diffusion [N6-R3]. That tradeoff is central to hydrogel design: increasing citric acid concentration increases crosslinking density but may decrease swelling and hydrophilicity [N6-R4]. In addition, some studies indicate that reaction time and crosslinking conditions affect the resulting hydrogel properties. For example, in the comparative study of citric acid and glutaraldehyde, hydrogel properties were influenced by the choice of crosslinking agent and by the incorporation of cellulose nanocrystals, which altered surface homogeneity and mechanical properties [N4-F4]. This implies that citric acid crosslinking is not inherently automatic and may require careful optimization of time, temperature, and catalysts.

Overall, citric acid is effective in hydrogels because it improves mechanical strength and thermal stability while preserving biocompatibility and biodegradability [N2-F2][N4-F4]. Its advantages make it especially suitable for biomedical and sustainable applications, but its limitations include the need for precise control of concentration, reaction time, and crosslinking density to avoid brittleness or excessive loss of swelling [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4].
node_outputs.N10:
Comparison with alternative crosslinkers and broader context

Citric acid compares favorably with glutaraldehyde and other crosslinkers in hydrogel systems, but the choice depends on the desired balance of mechanical strength, biocompatibility, environmental impact, and processability. In the comparative study of citric acid and glutaraldehyde, hydrogels crosslinked with glutaraldehyde showed higher mechanical strength, higher Young’s modulus, and greater rigidity, whereas citric acid hydrogels exhibited improved clarity, reduced water permeability, and enhanced swelling capacity [N4-F4]. That is a key tradeoff: glutaraldehyde is mechanically stronger but less environmentally friendly and potentially more toxic, while citric acid is more biocompatible, less toxic, and more sustainable [N4-F4]. The same study also notes that citric acid systems showed greater thermal stability, which is an important advantage for applications where heat resistance matters [N4-F4].

In the broader hydrogel context, citric acid is part of a family of multifunctional crosslinkers that are preferred when biocompatibility and sustainability are priorities. The hydrogel review states that natural crosslinking agents are preferred for hydrogels because they are similar to natural tissues, biocompatible, and less toxic [N2-F2]. It also lists multifunctional carboxylic acids among the most often used crosslinking agents for cellulose-based hydrogels [N2-F2]. In contrast, glutaraldehyde is highlighted as a widely used crosslinker that forms stable covalent bonds with amino and hydroxyl groups, but its toxicity when residues are not completely removed is a major limitation [N4-F4]. This means citric acid is often preferred in biomedical and environmentally sensitive applications, while glutaraldehyde may be more suitable when maximum mechanical strength and rapid crosslinking are required.

PEG and other crosslinkers are also relevant. The review notes that synthetic crosslinking agents can provide adjustable mechanical properties and easier chemical control, but natural crosslinking agents are better biocompatible and less toxic [N2-F2]. PEG is not directly compared in the provided evidence, but the general context implies that synthetic crosslinkers may offer tunability at the expense of biocompatibility and environmental friendliness [N2-F2]. In this broader context, citric acid stands out as a green, biocompatible, and multifunctional crosslinker that is well-suited to sustainable and biomedical applications [N2-F2][N4-F4].

The implications for scalability, processability, and application suitability are therefore clear. Citric acid is attractive because it is non-toxic, renewable, and compatible with many hydrophilic and biopolymer matrices [N2-F2][N4-F4]. Its reaction conditions can be tuned, as shown by studies on citric acid crosslinking of starch films and PVA/CA hydrogels [N5-R4][N7-R2]. However, scalability and processability depend on the system: while citric acid is environmentally friendly, achieving consistent crosslinking density may require precise control of concentration, temperature, and reaction time [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Overall, citric acid is preferred when biocompatibility, sustainability, and moderate swelling are important, while other crosslinkers may be more suitable when mechanical strength, rapid formation, or synthetic tunability are the priorities [N2-F2][N4-F4].
node_outputs.N8:
Core mechanism of citric acid crosslinking

Citric acid functions as a multifunctional crosslinker because it has multiple reactive sites. The esterification-based mechanism paper explains that citric acid is a tricarboxylic acid with two primary carboxyl groups and one tertiary carboxyl group, plus a tertiary hydroxyl group [N1-F1]. It also states that all three carboxyl groups of citric acid are reactive during esterification, which guarantees its ability to act as an eco-friendly crosslinker [N1-F1]. This multiple-reactive-site structure is central to its crosslinking effectiveness: each molecule can participate in several esterification reactions, allowing it to bridge multiple polymer chains rather than simply acting as a bivalent linker [N1-F1]. The review on polysaccharides and proteins also notes that crosslinking reaction mechanisms between crosslinkers and polysaccharides or proteins were revisited, reinforcing that citric acid is a well-characterized multifunctional crosslinker in hydrogel chemistry [N4-R3].

The specific chemical reactions involved are esterification, dehydration, and ring-opening. The esterification pathway is the most directly supported evidence here: the mechanism paper reports that citric acid can participate in esterification reactions with hydroxyl groups, and that tertiary carboxylic groups and hydroxyl groups of citric acid can form cross-links [N1-F1]. It also notes that esterification can occur at low temperature (<100 °C) and that CA self-catalyzed esterification may proceed via anhydride formation [N1-F1]. Another source explicitly describes citric acid crosslinking of PVA as involving esterification of the carboxyl group of citric acid with the hydroxyl group of PVA during heating and dehydration [N5-R3]. This shows that dehydration is not merely a side reaction but an integral part of the crosslinking mechanism, as the formation of ester bonds often requires loss of water [N5-R3]. A related paper on citric acid crosslinking of starch films similarly states that citric acid plays a crosslinking role effective through esterification reactions between its carboxyl groups and hydroxyl groups [N5-R4]. These sources together support a mechanism in which citric acid forms ester linkages by reacting with hydroxyl groups, with dehydration playing a key role in stabilizing the crosslinked network [N1-F1][N5-R3].

pH and temperature affect reaction kinetics and crosslinking efficiency. The mechanism paper explicitly reports a kinetic study of the esterification reaction of citric acid and butyl glycol with and without catalyst [N7-R4], showing that reaction conditions are important. The same paper also notes that esterification can occur at low temperature (<100 °C) and that anhydride formation may be part of the pathway [N1-F1]. Another source reports that citric acid crosslinking of paper products can be used to improve wet strength, and that more than one carboxyl group in one citric acid molecule can react with protein in aqueous medium at pH 6.8 under 50 and 75 °C conditions [N7-R1]. This indicates that pH and temperature are not only important for reaction selectivity but also for the extent and rate of crosslinking. The hydrogel review also notes that chemical crosslinking can increase thermal stability, strength, toughness, and transform thermoplastics into thermosets [N2-F2], which further supports the idea that reaction conditions influence final crosslinked properties. In short, citric acid crosslinking is driven by esterification and dehydration, with crosslinking efficiency being sensitive to pH and temperature [N1-F1][N5-R3][N7-R1].
node_outputs.N11:
Crosslinking density and hydrogel performance tradeoffs

Increasing citric acid concentration generally increases crosslinking density, but the relationship is nonlinear and depends on the system. The evidence shows that the addition of citric acid lower than 40% cannot create crosslinked networks, so hydrogels cannot form and become brittle [N6-R1]. At 40% citric acid, crosslinked networks begin to form, indicating that a threshold concentration is required for network formation [N6-R1]. A separate source reports that higher concentration of CMC and citric acid increased cross-linking density, and high cross-linking density significantly decreased the swelling capacity [N6-R4]. This implies that citric acid concentration is a direct driver of crosslinking density, with more crosslinker leading to more dense networks, but also to less swelling.

The tradeoffs between mechanical strength, swelling, and hydrophilicity are clear. The hydrogel review states that chemical crosslinking can increase thermal stability, strength, toughness, and transform thermoplastics into thermosets [N2-F2]. In citric acid crosslinked systems, the review also notes that higher crosslinking density can reduce water absorption because the polymer network acts as a barrier to water diffusion [N6-R3]. This is consistent with the broader tradeoff: denser networks improve mechanical rigidity and stability, but reduce the hydrogel’s ability to swell and absorb water [N6-R3][N6-R4]. The same review emphasizes that if the amount of crosslinking agent is too small, the hydrogel becomes brittle; if too much is used, the crosslinking degree causes a low swelling degree [N2-F2]. That means crosslinking density is a continuous tradeoff: too little gives weak or brittle hydrogels, while too much makes them rigid and less water-absorbing [N2-F2][N6-R3].

Hydrophilicity is also affected. The mechanism-based evidence shows that citric acid participates in esterification reactions, with dehydration playing a key role in crosslinking [N1-F1][N5-R3]. Because esterification often requires removal of water, the resulting network becomes less hydrophilic as crosslinking increases [N5-R3]. In addition, the review notes that citric acid crosslinked hydrogels can have improved clarity and reduced water permeability, while also showing greater thermal stability [N4-F4]. This suggests that higher crosslinking density can shift the hydrogel toward a more hydrophobic or less permeable state, which may be desirable for certain applications but undesirable for others that require high water absorption or hydrophilic behavior [N4-F4][N6-R3].

Crosslinking density also affects hydrogel stability and failure modes. ## What makes citric acid an effective crosslinking agent in hydrogel synthesis?

Citric acid is effective as a crosslinking agent in hydrogel synthesis because it combines multifunctionality, biocompatibility, and tunable network formation. It is a tricarboxylic acid with multiple reactive sites, making it capable of bridging polymer chains through multiple crosslinks rather than acting as a simple bivalent linker [N1-F1][N4-R3]. This structural versatility is central to its effectiveness: citric acid can participate in esterification reactions with hydroxyl groups, and it has been shown to have three reactive carboxyl groups and a tertiary hydroxyl group, all of which contribute to crosslinking [N1-F1][N5-R3][N5-R4]. The evidence also supports esterification and dehydration as key parts of the crosslinking mechanism, with dehydration playing an important role in stabilizing the crosslinked network [N1-F1][N5-R3]. Together, these properties allow citric acid to form a dense, covalent network that strengthens the hydrogel while preserving some degree of hydrophilicity and processability [N1-F1][N4-R3].

## Why citric acid works well in hydrogel synthesis

The main reason citric acid is effective is that it improves both network formation and hydrogel stability. In cellulose-based hydrogels, citric acid is described as a non-toxic crosslinking agent that produces hydrogels with good swelling capabilities and biodegradability [N2-F2]. The same review notes that chemical crosslinking can increase thermal stability, strength, toughness, and transform thermoplastics into thermosets [N2-F2]. That means citric acid is not only a means of creating a network but also a way to enhance the physical robustness of the hydrogel. The comparative study of citric acid and glutaraldehyde further shows that citric acid systems can exhibit improved clarity, reduced water permeability, and enhanced swelling capacity, while also showing greater thermal stability [N4-F4]. This combination of rigidity and swelling control is especially valuable in hydrogel design, where the material must balance mechanical integrity with functionality.

## The underlying mechanisms involved

The mechanism of citric acid crosslinking is based on esterification and dehydration. The esterification-based mechanism paper explains that citric acid is a tricarboxylic acid with two primary carboxyl groups and one tertiary carboxyl group, plus a tertiary hydroxyl group [N1-F1]. It also states that all three carboxyl groups of citric acid are reactive during esterification, which guarantees its ability to act as an eco-friendly crosslinker [N1-F1]. In practice, citric acid crosslinks by reacting with hydroxyl groups on polymer chains, forming ester bonds [N5-R3][N5-R4]. The review on polysaccharides and proteins also notes that crosslinking reaction mechanisms between crosslinkers and polysaccharides or proteins were revisited, reinforcing that citric acid is a well-characterized multifunctional crosslinker in hydrogel chemistry [N4-R3].

Dehydration is an important part of the process. The same esterification mechanism paper reports that CA self-catalyzed esterification may proceed via anhydride formation, and that esterification can occur at low temperature (<100 °C) [N1-F1]. A separate source describes citric acid crosslinking of PVA as involving esterification of the carboxyl group of citric acid with the hydroxyl group of PVA during heating and dehydration [N5-R3]. This shows that dehydration is not merely a side reaction but an integral part of the crosslinking mechanism, as the formation of ester bonds often requires loss of water [N5-R3]. In addition, the paper on citric acid crosslinking of starch films states that citric acid plays a crosslinking role effective through esterification reactions between its carboxyl groups and hydroxyl groups [N5-R4]. Taken together, these sources support a mechanism in which citric acid forms ester linkages by reacting with hydroxyl groups, with dehydration playing a key role in stabilizing the crosslinked network [N1-F1][N5-R3].

Reaction conditions also affect crosslinking efficiency. The mechanism paper explicitly reports a kinetic study of the esterification reaction of citric acid and butyl glycol with and without catalyst [N7-R4], showing that reaction kinetics are important. It also notes that esterification can occur at low temperature (<100 °C) and that anhydride formation may be part of the pathway [N1-F1]. Another source reports that citric acid crosslinking of paper products can be used to improve wet strength, and that more than one carboxyl group in one citric acid molecule can react with protein in aqueous medium at pH 6.8 under 50 and 75 °C conditions [N7-R1]. In hydrogel-specific terms, citric acid is attractive because it improves mechanical strength, swelling, and stability while maintaining biocompatibility and biodegradability [N2-F2][N4-F4]. These findings support the idea that citric acid is a safer alternative to more toxic crosslinkers in biomedical contexts [N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2].

Despite its advantages, citric acid has practical limitations that must be managed. One major limitation is the need to control concentration carefully. Citric acid compares favorably with glutaraldehyde and other crosslinkers in hydrogel systems, but the choice depends on the desired balance of mechanical strength, biocompatibility, environmental impact, and processability [N4-F4][N2-F2]. In the comparative study of citric acid and glutaraldehyde, hydrogels crosslinked with glutaraldehyde showed higher mechanical strength, higher Young’s modulus, and greater rigidity, whereas citric acid hydrogels exhibited improved clarity, reduced water permeability, and enhanced swelling capacity [N4-F4]. That is a key tradeoff: glutaraldehyde is mechanically stronger but less environmentally friendly and potentially more toxic, while citric acid is more biocompatible, less toxic, and more sustainable [N4-F4]. The same study also notes that citric acid systems showed greater thermal stability, which is an important advantage for applications where heat resistance matters [N4-F4].

In the broader hydrogel context, citric acid is part of a family of multifunctional crosslinkers that are preferred when biocompatibility and sustainability are priorities [N2-F2][N4-R3]. The hydrogel review states that natural crosslinking agents are preferred for hydrogels because they are similar to natural tissues, biocompatible, and less toxic [N2-F2]. It also lists multifunctional carboxylic acids among the most often used crosslinking agents for cellulose-based hydrogels [N2-F2]. Glutaraldehyde is highlighted as a widely used crosslinker that forms stable covalent bonds with amino and hydroxyl groups, but its toxicity when residues are not completely removed is a major limitation [N4-F4]. This means citric acid is often preferred in biomedical and environmentally sensitive applications, while glutaraldehyde may be more suitable when maximum mechanical strength and rapid crosslinking are required [N2-F2][N4-F4].

PEG and other crosslinkers are also relevant. The review notes that synthetic crosslinking agents can provide adjustable mechanical properties and easier chemical control, but natural crosslinking agents are better biocompatible and less toxic [N2-F2]. PEG is not directly compared in the provided evidence, but the general context implies that synthetic crosslinkers may offer tunability at the expense of biocompatibility and environmental friendliness [N2-F2]. In this broader context, citric acid stands out as a green, biocompatible, and multifunctional crosslinker that is well-suited to sustainable and biomedical applications [N2-F2][N4-F4].

## Implications for scalability, processability, and application suitability

The implications for scalability, processability, and application suitability are therefore clear. Citric acid is attractive because it is non-toxic, renewable, and compatible with many hydrophilic and biopolymer matrices [N2-F2][N4-F4]. Its reaction conditions can be tuned, as shown by studies on citric acid crosslinking of starch films and PVA/CA hydrogels [N5-R4][N7-R2]. However, scalability and processability depend on the system: while citric acid is environmentally friendly, achieving consistent crosslinking density may require precise control of concentration, temperature, and reaction time [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Overall, citric acid is preferred when biocompatibility, sustainability, and moderate swelling are important, while other crosslinkers may be more suitable when mechanical strength, rapid formation, or synthetic tunability are the priorities [N2-F2][N4-F4].

## Crosslinking density and hydrogel performance tradeoffs

Increasing citric acid concentration generally increases crosslinking density, but the relationship is nonlinear and depends on the system. The evidence shows that the addition of citric acid lower than 40% cannot create crosslinked networks, so hydrogels cannot form and become brittle [N6-R1]. At 40% citric acid, crosslinked networks begin to form, indicating that a threshold concentration is required for network formation [N6-R1]. A separate source reports that higher concentration of CMC and citric acid increased cross-linking density, and high cross-linking density significantly decreased the swelling capacity [N6-R4]. This implies that citric acid concentration is a direct driver of crosslinking density, with more crosslinker leading to more dense networks, but also to less swelling.

The tradeoffs between mechanical strength, swelling, and hydrophilicity are clear. The hydrogel review states that chemical crosslinking can increase thermal stability, strength, toughness, and transform thermoplastics into thermosets [N2-F2]. In citric acid crosslinked systems, the review also notes that higher crosslinking density can reduce water absorption because the polymer network acts as a barrier to water diffusion [N6-R3]. This is consistent with the broader tradeoff: denser networks improve mechanical rigidity and stability, but reduce the hydrogel’s ability to swell and absorb water [N6-R3][N6-R4]. The same review emphasizes that if the amount of crosslinking agent is too small, the hydrogel becomes brittle; if too much is used, the crosslinking degree causes a low swelling degree [N2-F2]. That means crosslinking density is a continuous tradeoff: too little gives weak or brittle hydrogels, while too much makes them rigid and less water-absorbing [N2-F2][N6-R3].

Hydrophilicity is also affected. The mechanism-based evidence shows that citric acid participates in esterification reactions, with dehydration playing a key role in crosslinking [N1-F1][N5-R3]. Because esterification often requires removal of water, the resulting network becomes less hydrophilic as crosslinking increases [N5-R3]. In addition, the review notes that citric acid crosslinked hydrogels can have improved clarity and reduced water permeability, while also showing greater thermal stability [N4-F4]. This suggests that higher crosslinking density can shift the hydrogel toward a more hydrophobic or less permeable state, which may be desirable for certain applications but undesirable for others that require high water absorption or hydrophilic behavior [N4-F4][N6-R3].

Crosslinking density also affects hydrogel stability and failure modes. The review states that crosslinking can increase thermal stability, strength, and toughness, and can transform thermoplastics into thermosets [N2-F2]. This means that higher crosslinking density generally improves mechanical and thermal stability, making the hydrogel more durable under stress. However, the same review warns that excessive crosslinking can make the hydrogel less swellable and more brittle [N2-F2]. The evidence on starch-crosslinked systems further supports this: citric acid crosslinking delayed microbial growth and extended film longevity by 20% [N3-R1], suggesting that moderate crosslinking can enhance long-term stability. At the same time, the hydrogel review explicitly states that too much crosslinking agent can lead to a high crosslinking degree and a low swelling degree [N2-F2], which may increase the risk of brittleness and failure under mechanical loading.

## Bottom line

Citric acid is effective as a crosslinking agent in hydrogel synthesis because it is a multifunctional, biocompatible, and tunable crosslinker. It functions through multiple reactive sites, forming ester bonds with hydroxyl groups and involving dehydration as part of the reaction pathway [N1-F1][N5-R3][N5-R4]. Its ability to improve mechanical strength, thermal stability, and hydrogel rigidity, while also preserving some swelling capacity, makes it especially attractive for biomedical and sustainable applications [N2-F2][N4-F4]. However, its effectiveness depends on careful control of concentration, temperature, and reaction conditions, because higher crosslinking density increases rigidity but may reduce swelling and hydrophilicity [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Compared with glutaraldehyde and other crosslinkers, citric acid is preferred when biocompatibility, sustainability, and moderate swelling are important, while other crosslinkers may be more suitable when maximum mechanical strength or synthetic tunability are the priority [N2-F2][N4-F4]. Overall, citric acid’s combination of reactivity, biocompatibility, and tunable network formation makes it a powerful choice for hydrogel synthesis, but its performance must be balanced against the tradeoffs imposed by crosslinking density [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4].
